title: Weighing Bench
context: Grade 4, and the first time the chapter's pattern comes round again. An adult sees the length work done with a new unit. What is actually being taught is that this pair has one number only. The page's summary box after the weight conversions is the length box copied word for word: multiply or divide by 10, 100 or 1000. For grams and kilograms the only number is a thousand, and a child who follows the box writes three kilograms as three hundred grams.

writeup.why: Sort things into grams or kilograms, see that a thousand grams make a kilogram, and change weights both ways by a thousand only.
writeup.look: A pan balance with a shelf of things at the left, a converter with one number on it at the right, and a place board below.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Weighing Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the things sorted or the cards passed against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each thing settles in a tray or each card comes through, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the second phase it counts the hundred gram weights added and shows no second number, because how many level the kilogram is the thing being found. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The thing shelf stands at the top left of the working area, 460 by 90 at 64,214, holding a spoon, a letter, a bunch of keys, a bag of cement and a sack of onions, each drawn plainly. The pan balance stands under it, 460 by 280 at 64,320: a near-black beam on a post with a pan hanging from each end. The beam tilts toward the heavier pan and levels only when the two loads weigh the same, and a small near-black arrow under it points to the pan that has gone down. A kilogram weight is a deep blue iron block marked 1 kg, and a gram weight is a small green block marked 100 g; the grams set on a pan are counted in that pan's own counter under it. The grams tray and the kilograms tray stand under the balance, each 220 by 100, at 64,620 and 304,620, labelled in ink. At the right the converter stands, 380 by 200 at 560,214, a machine with one number printed on its front, a thousand, and no dial or setting for any other number; a weight card, 360 by 80, goes in at its top and comes out at its foot. Passed through going down, a card in kilograms and grams comes out in grams, the kilograms multiplied by a thousand and the grams added on. Passed back going up, a card in grams is divided by a thousand, and the quotient lands in the kilograms slot, 170 by 70 at 560,440, and the remainder in the grams slot, 170 by 70 at 770,440, written as a number, where it stays. The place board runs under them, 560 by 110 at 560,560, four boxes headed thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, with a fifth box for ten thousands that opens only when a weight needs it, and a box the grams leave empty takes a grey zero at full size. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with no dot key, and a unit tag under the slot reading grams or kilograms, filled in beside the number and never left off. On the first phase a word pad sits over it with two keys, grams and kilograms. On the third the slot is a card of two parts, kilograms and grams, with the unit names printed beside them. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green: metres beside kilometres, centimetres beside metres, millimetres, grams and millilitres. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that fills an empty place of the smaller unit is grey. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape, and the mark where a reading is taken, are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket, strike line, table rule and panel edge, is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, and a count by the slot that names what is counted, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in the smaller unit's places is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A figure that goes down by one when a unit is broken is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. No measure in two units is written as a decimal anywhere on the stage. The converter carries one number and has no way to set another, so grams and kilograms are joined here only by a thousand. The beam is drawn to tip toward the heavier pan and to level only for equal loads, so the pan that goes down is the pan holding the heavier load.
writeup.finish: The card shows the two trays with the things the child sorted, the levelled balance, and the last card with its kilograms and grams slots and place board.

phases.win: each thing settles in its tray, the light ones in grams and the heavy ones in kilograms
phases.does: lifts each thing onto the pan and sends it to the tray for its unit
phases.goal: heavy things are weighed in kilograms and light things in grams
phases.says: Is it heavy or light? Grams or kilograms?
phases.check: Away from the screen: would you weigh a school bag in grams or kilograms? And a pencil?
phases.feels: the balance tips toward the heavier thing, and heavy things go with kilograms
phases.hands: Let children lift pairs of things, a school bag and a pencil, a water bottle and an eraser, and say which is heavier. Sort a pile of things into heavy and light on two sheets marked kilograms and grams. If the school has a pan balance, put a kilogram packet on one pan and a light thing on the other, and ask which pan went down and why.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: is the thing heavy or light in the hand? Second rung, the phase's: which pan went down? Third rung: the shelf is cut to one heavy thing and one light one, and the child weighs them against each other before the other things come back. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: higher often means more, as a taller stack or a taller bar does, and the keys' pan is the higher one.
wrong.move: reads the pan holding the keys, riding high, as the heavier one, and sends the keys to kilograms.
wrong.screen: the beam is drawn again with the small near-black arrow under it lit, pointing to the pan that has gone down, the kilogram's. The keys go to the grams tray beside the spoon and the letter, and the child's choice stays lit on the word pad, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the unit is picked from the number the child wants to write, not from how heavy the thing is.
wrong.move: gives the sack of onions a weight of twenty grams, because twenty is a small, easy number.
wrong.screen: twenty grams is set on the other pan as one small green weight, and the sack's pan stays down and does not stir. Kilogram weights then go on one at a time, and the sack's pan stays down under several of them, and the kilograms tray lights. The child's twenty grams stays on the pad beside it.

phases.screen: the shelf of things, the grams tray and the kilograms tray
phases.soWhat: Heavy things are usually weighed in kilograms and light things in grams. On a pan balance, the pan that goes down holds the heavier load.

phases.win: the pans level at a thousand grams, and the card comes out in grams
phases.does: adds hundred gram weights until the pans level, counts the grams, then passes a card in kilograms through the converter
phases.goal: a kilogram is a thousand grams, so kilograms become grams by multiplying by a thousand, and only by a thousand
phases.says: How many grams level the kilogram? Now use that number.
phases.check: How many grams are there in 7 kg? And in 7 kg 60 g?
phases.feels: a kilogram and a thousand grams balance exactly, so there is one number to use
phases.hands: Put a one kilogram packet on one pan of a school balance and add hundred gram packets to the other one at a time, counting the grams aloud: one hundred, two hundred, and on. Stop when the pans are level and write the total. Then ask how many grams nine kilogram packets would balance, and write nine thousand.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what number is printed on the converter? Second rung, the phase's: how many grams levelled one kilogram? Third rung: the card is cut to one kilogram, and the child levels it on the balance before the larger card comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the summary box printed after the weight conversions copies the length box and offers a hundred among its numbers, though for grams and kilograms the only number is a thousand.
wrong.move: writes nine hundred grams for nine kilograms, multiplying by a hundred.
wrong.screen: the converter's one number, a thousand, lights on its front. Nine kilogram weights go on one pan and nine hundred grams of hundred gram weights on the other, and the beam stays tipped hard toward the kilograms. The card then passes through, nine times a thousand, nine thousand grams, and the child's nine hundred stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the multiplying feels like the whole job, and the grams on the card look done already.
wrong.move: multiplies the kilograms and leaves the grams behind, writing four thousand grams for four kilograms three hundred and seventy-five grams.
wrong.screen: the three hundred and seventy-five grams stay lit on the card at the converter's top after the four thousand have come out. They then drop through after it, already grams, and join the four thousand, and the card reads four thousand three hundred and seventy-five grams. The child's four thousand stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: a kilogram weight on one pan and a pile of hundred gram weights beside the other
phases.soWhat: A thousand grams make a kilogram. Kilograms become grams by multiplying by a thousand, and only by a thousand, with any grams added on.
phases.concept: A thousand grams make a kilogram

phases.win: the kilograms and the grams stand in their slots and rebuild the card together
phases.does: passes the card back through the converter and reads the two slots
phases.goal: divide by a thousand; the quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams
phases.says: How many whole kilograms are in it? What is left stays in grams.
phases.check: Write 8315 g in kilograms and grams. What is the remainder, and which slot does it go in?
phases.feels: the whole kilograms come out, and the grams that cannot make another kilogram stay grams
phases.hands: Write 3615 g on the board. Ask how many whole kilograms are in it, counting in thousands: one thousand, two thousand, three thousand. Ask what is left over, six hundred and fifteen, and whether it could make another kilogram. Write three kilograms six hundred and fifteen grams, and check it by putting the three thousand and the six hundred and fifteen back together.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many grams make one kilogram? Second rung, the phase's: how many whole kilograms fit, and what is left? Third rung: the card is cut to a little more than one kilogram, and the child passes it back before the larger card returns. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a hundred was the number for metres and centimetres, and dividing by it has become a habit.
wrong.move: divides by a hundred and writes fifty-two kilograms forty grams for five thousand two hundred and forty grams.
wrong.screen: the converter's one number, a thousand, lights, and the card passes back through it: five whole kilograms land in the kilograms slot and two hundred and forty grams stay in the grams slot. The child's fifty-two kilograms is set beside it as fifty-two kilogram weights, a heap far larger than the card, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the whole kilograms are the answer to the dividing, and what is left over looks finished with.
wrong.move: writes five kilograms and stops, leaving the two hundred and forty grams out.
wrong.screen: the grams slot holds two hundred and forty in green, lit, beside the five kilograms. The two slots are put back together through the converter, five thousand grams and two hundred and forty grams, and the card is whole again. The child's five kilograms stays in the slot, two hundred and forty grams short.

phases.screen: a card in grams alone, and the empty kilograms and grams slots
phases.soWhat: Grams become kilograms and grams by dividing by a thousand. The quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams.

phases.win: a zero drops into every empty box and the grams read correctly
phases.does: passes the card into grams and writes it on the place board, one digit to a box
phases.goal: when the grams do not fill three places, a zero holds each empty one
phases.says: The grams leave some places empty. What goes in each one?
phases.check: Write 2 kg 5 g in grams. Which places hold zeros?
phases.feels: the empty places do not vanish; each one waits for a zero
phases.hands: Draw four boxes on the board headed thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Ask the class to write five kilograms six grams in grams, one digit to a box: the five goes in the thousands and the six in the ones. Point to the two empty boxes and ask what goes in them. Then do three kilograms forty grams the same way.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which boxes do the grams fill? Second rung, the phase's: which boxes are still empty? Third rung: the card is cut to one kilogram and a few grams, and the child fills the board before the larger card comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: zeros usually come at the end of a number, as in five thousand, so the empty places seem to belong there.
wrong.move: writes five thousand six hundred grams for five kilograms six grams, setting the six straight after the five and filling the end with zeros.
wrong.screen: the place board takes the five in its thousands box and the six in its ones box, because six grams are six ones, and grey zeros drop into the hundreds and the tens at full size: five thousand and six. The child's number is laid on a second board beside it, five hundred and ninety-four grams more, and both stay drawn.

wrong.why: the two parts are said one after the other, three and forty, so they are written one after the other.
wrong.move: writes three hundred and forty grams for three kilograms forty grams, setting the digits side by side as they are said.
wrong.screen: the child's three hundred and forty is laid on the place board, the three standing in the hundreds box, three hundred grams, less than one kilogram. The card then passes through, three thousand grams and forty more, and a grey zero drops into the empty hundreds box. The two boards stand side by side, two thousand seven hundred grams apart.

phases.screen: a card in kilograms and a small number of grams, and the place board with four empty boxes
phases.soWhat: Beside kilograms the grams take three places, and a zero holds each place they leave empty.
phases.concept: A zero that holds a place in grams

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the last hundred gram weight goes on. The beam, tipped hard toward the kilogram, stays tipped as each weight is added, and on the last one it lifts, wobbles and settles dead level, and the counter under the pan reads one thousand grams. Then the kilogram weight and the pile of gram weights swap pans in one slow arc, and the beam stays level. It can be tried again as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the shelf holds its five things, a kilogram weight sits on the right pan and the two trays stand empty. On the second the kilogram weight sits on one pan with a pile of hundred gram weights beside the other, the beam tipped down toward the kilogram. On the third a card in grams alone waits at the converter's foot, with the kilograms slot and the grams slot empty. On the fourth a card in kilograms and a small number of grams waits at the converter's top, above the place board's four empty boxes. The running count at the top left holds the things sorted or the cards passed against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the spoon, or the first hundred gram weight, or the card, or the hundreds box, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks whether each thing is heavy or light. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any thing from the shelf on the balance, and any weight up to ninety-nine kilograms through the converter either way, with the place board open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on choosing grams or kilograms, kilograms into grams, grams into kilograms and grams, and zeros that hold empty places in the grams.
voiceLines: A balance and a shelf of things. Is each one heavy or light?
Is it heavy or light? Grams or kilograms?
How many grams level the kilogram? Now use that number.
How many whole kilograms are in it? What is left stays in grams.
The grams leave some places empty. What goes in each one?
A new weight. Is it in kilograms, in grams, or in both?
Free play. Anything on the balance, and any weight through the converter either way.
Lift it again and watch the balance, or read the one number on the converter.
Every thing weighed in a unit that suits it, and every weight changed by a thousand, the remainder kept as grams.

observations.why: The pan that goes down holds the heavier load, and the keys were lighter than the kilogram.
observations.soWhat: Heavy things are usually weighed in kilograms and light things in grams. Choose the unit that suits the thing.
observations.observe: The keys' pan rode up against the kilogram weight, and the keys went to grams with the spoon and the letter.

observations.why: A kilogram weighs the same as a thousand grams, so they balance.
observations.soWhat: A thousand grams make a kilogram, so kilograms become grams by multiplying by a thousand, and only by a thousand.
observations.observe: The beam levelled when the hundred gram weights on one pan came to a thousand grams.

observations.why: The grams left over were fewer than a thousand, not enough for another kilogram.
observations.soWhat: Grams become kilograms and grams by dividing by a thousand. The quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams.
observations.observe: Passed back through the converter, the whole kilograms landed in one slot and the grams left over stayed in the other.

observations.why: Beside kilograms the grams take three places, and six grams fill only the ones.
observations.soWhat: A zero holds each place the grams leave empty, so five kilograms six grams is five thousand and six grams.
observations.observe: Six grams went into the ones box, and zeros dropped into the hundreds and the tens.

source_tool.description: A pan balance stands at the left of the stage with a shelf of everyday things beside it, a spoon, a letter, a bunch of keys, a bag of cement and a sack of onions. A thing lifted onto the pan settles into a grams tray or a kilograms tray by how heavy it is. A kilogram weight on one pan is levelled by gram weights on the other, added a hundred grams at a time, until a thousand grams balance it. At the right a converter joins the two units with one number only, a thousand, and has no setting for any other number. A weight card in kilograms and grams passes through it into grams: the kilograms are multiplied by a thousand and the grams added on. A weight card in grams passes back: it is divided by a thousand, the quotient lands in the kilograms slot and the remainder stays in the grams slot. A place board below shows the grams in thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, with a zero in every place the grams leave empty.
source_tool.art_direction: A pan balance levelling one kilogram / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a workbench with a tray of everyday things, a fifteen centimetre ruler, a ladder of units, a column frame with a unit switch, a pan balance with iron weights, a tap, jugs, glasses, jars, bottles and a tank.

A ruler is drawn as the page draws it: a long tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen, and a first tick carrying the unit name and no numeral. That first tick is the zero mark and lights as one.
Every measure is written with its unit named, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, as in 4 km 66 m. A measure in two units is never written as a decimal on any stage.

The smaller unit's places are fixed boxes: three beside kilometres, kilograms and litres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres. A zero filling one of those boxes is drawn at full size and weight and is never dimmed or dropped.

A number that joins two units is shown beside them wherever the child works with them: ten between millimetres and centimetres, a hundred between centimetres and metres, and a thousand between metres and kilometres, grams and kilograms, and millilitres and litres. Weight and capacity carry one number only, a thousand.
What is left after dividing is drawn in its own slot in the smaller unit, at full strength, and it is never folded into the quotient.

A larger unit broken to borrow is drawn as exactly the joining number of smaller pieces: ten pieces for a centimetre, a hundred for a metre, and a thousand for a kilometre, a kilogram or a litre, the thousand drawn as ten bars of a hundred.
No count, reading or result is shown before the child makes it. A jar count appears only once the pouring is done, and a reading only once the object is laid.
Every word on the stage says weight, the vocabulary box's word, for how heavy a thing is.
A container whose capacity is shown is drawn full to its brim.
Two measures being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a bar, a weight or a liquid the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that pads the smaller unit's places, as in zero seven five, is grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded, because it is holding a place. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape and the mark where a reading is taken are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket and table rule, is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because each unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, and a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

phase_map.concept: A thousand grams make a kilogram
A zero that holds a place in grams

placement.where: After things have been lifted in the hand and sorted into heavy and light, and a kilogram packet has been balanced against smaller packets on a real pan balance. The tool is what joins grams and kilograms by a thousand only, where the summary box offers ten, a hundred or a thousand.

answer_key.rule: Heavy things are weighed in kilograms and light things in grams. A thousand grams make a kilogram, and a thousand is the only number that joins grams and kilograms. Kilograms become grams by multiplying by a thousand, with any grams added on. Grams become kilograms and grams by dividing by a thousand: the quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams. Beside kilograms, grams take three places, and a zero holds any place the grams leave empty, so 8 kg 50 g is 8050 g.
answer_key.wrong: The converter's one number, a thousand, lights, the card is passed through again, and the balance levels a kilogram against a thousand grams beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A bag of cement is heavy, too heavy to lift easily.
Heavy things are weighed in kilograms, so the cement is weighed in kilograms.
A spoon is light, and light things are weighed in grams.
items.answer: The bag of cement in kilograms, and the spoon in grams
items.question: Which unit suits each weight: a bag of cement, and a steel spoon?
items.checkpoint: Heavy things are weighed in kilograms and light things in grams.
items.misconception: Choosing the unit by the size of the number to be written, not by how heavy the thing is.

steps: A kilogram is a thousand grams.
9 times 1000 is 9000, so 9 kg is 9000 g.
items.question: How many grams are there in 9 kg?
items.checkpoint: Kilograms become grams by multiplying by a thousand, and only by a thousand.
items.misconception: Multiplying by a hundred and writing 900 g, because the summary box offers ten, a hundred or a thousand; for grams the only number is a thousand.

steps: A thousand grams make a kilogram, so divide 6385 by 1000.
The quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams: 6 kg 385 g. Check: 6000 add 385 is 6385.
items.question: Write 6385 g in kilograms and grams.
items.checkpoint: Grams become kilograms and grams by dividing by a thousand; the remainder stays as grams.
items.misconception: Dividing by a hundred and writing 63 kg 85 g, as if grams joined kilograms the way centimetres join metres.

steps: 7 kg is 7 times 1000 g, which is 7000 g.
The 9 g fill the ones place, so the hundreds and the tens are empty.
Zeros hold the hundreds and the tens: 7000 g and 9 g make 7009 g.
items.question: Write 7 kg 9 g in grams.
items.checkpoint: Beside kilograms, grams take three places, and a zero holds any place they leave empty.
items.misconception: Writing 79 g, or 7900 g, with no zeros holding the empty places.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Grams or kilograms: a letter in an envelope, and a sack of onions?
items.final_answer: The letter in grams, and the sack of onions in kilograms

items.question: A child weighs an eraser and writes 20 kg. Which unit should it be?
items.final_answer: 20 g. An eraser is light, so it is weighed in grams

items.question: Convert 13 kg 640 g into grams.
items.final_answer: 13,640 g. 13 kg is 13,000 g, and 640 g more makes 13,640 g

items.question: Write 2750 g in kilograms and grams.
A sack of rice weighs 25,400 g. How many kilograms and grams is that?
items.final_answer: 25 kg 400 g, because 25,400 divided by 1000 is 25 remainder 400

items.question: Write 30 kg 8 g in grams.
items.final_answer: 30,008 g. Zeros hold the hundreds and the tens of the grams

items.question: A child writes 4070 g as 4 kg 700 g. What went wrong, and what is right?
items.final_answer: Dividing by 1000 leaves a remainder of 70, read from the last three digits 070, whose zero holds the hundreds. The weight is 4 kg 70 g

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the everyday things to be weighed
levels a kilogram weight against gram weights added a hundred grams at a time
take the light things and the heavy things
joins grams and kilograms by a thousand only
a weight in kilograms and grams, or in grams alone
take the quotient and the remainder after dividing by a thousand
shows the grams in four places, with a zero in every empty one

teaching_notes: Let the class lift things in their hands and sort them into heavy and light before the tool is opened. Then balance a kilogram packet against smaller packets on a real pan balance if the school has one. The page pictures five weighing instruments and asks for no reading from any of them, and the one captioned as a digital scale is drawn with a dial. The tick table asks whether four things are weighed in kilograms or grams. The summary box after Examples 11 and 12 copies the length box word for word and offers ten, a hundred or a thousand; for grams the only number is a thousand. A child who follows the box writes three kilograms as three hundred grams. Say a thousand, and only a thousand, every time. The page writes a division by a thousand that leaves a remainder as equal to a weight in two units; the quotient is the kilograms and the remainder stays as grams. Example 11 starts from seven point three two five kilograms. Seven point three two five is seven and three hundred and twenty-five thousandths, and a thousandth of a kilogram is a gram, so it is seven kilograms three hundred and twenty-five grams. Ask nothing more with decimals. Exercise 11.3 has sixty-five kilograms forty-five grams, which is sixty-five thousand and forty-five grams, with a zero in the hundreds. Say weight throughout, the vocabulary box's word.
generation_prompt: Build a weighing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A pan balance stands at the left of the working area with a shelf beside it holding a spoon, a letter, a bunch of keys, a bag of cement and a sack of onions. A thing dragged onto a pan settles into a grams tray or a kilograms tray below by how heavy it is. A kilogram iron weight can be set on one pan and hundred gram weights added to the other one at a time, the beam tilting toward the heavier pan and levelling only at a thousand grams, with a counter of the grams added. At the right of the canvas a converter joins g and kg by one number only, a thousand, printed on it, with no setting for any other number. A weight card in kg and g passed through it comes out in g, the kilograms multiplied by a thousand and the grams added on. A card in g passed back is divided by a thousand, the quotient landing in a kg slot and the remainder in a g slot, at full size. A place board below shows the grams in thousands, hundreds, tens and ones boxes, and every box the grams leave empty takes a zero drawn at the same size as the other digits. Every label says weight. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Lift a thing onto the pan. Send it to grams or kilograms. Level the kilogram with gram weights. Multiply or divide by a thousand only. The remainder stays in grams.
